analysis.one_liner: Eases bankruptcy rules for people overwhelmed by medical bills so they can keep their homes and erase more debt.
analysis.headline: The bill has been referred to two House committees, has one cosponsor, and has seen no committee action since its July 14, 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal bankruptcy law for people whose debts came from a serious illness or injury. A "medically distressed debtor" — someone who, in the past three years, paid out medical bills over 10% of their income (or $10,000), or lost wages because they or a close family member got sick — would get a lighter path through bankruptcy: a bigger home protection worth up to $250,000, no income means test, no required credit counseling, easier discharge of student loans, and a bankruptcy that never shows up on their credit report. People would have to sign a sworn statement that they did not run up medical bills on purpose to qualify. The bill was introduced in July 2026, referred to two House committees, and has one cosponsor; no committee has acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are forced into bankruptcy by medical bills — including unpaid bills for themselves, a spouse, a child, a parent, or a sibling, and people who lost jobs or hours because of illness or caregiving. For them, the bill would mean keeping up to $250,000 of home equity through a bankruptcy, skipping the means test and required credit counseling, wiping out student loans alongside medical debt, and keeping the bankruptcy off their credit reports so it does not follow them into future housing, jobs, and loans [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It exempts up to $250,000 in home equity (or other residential property, or a burial plot) for medically distressed debtors, in place of the much lower federal homestead exemption, so a family can keep its house through a bankruptcy.
It waives the Chapter 7 means test, which currently forces higher-income debtors into a five-year repayment plan rather than a fresh start, for medically distressed debtors.

It excuses medically distressed debtors from the strict Chapter 13 disposable-income requirement and from the pre-filing credit counseling session, removing procedural hurdles that exist to screen out casual filers rather than genuinely ill ones.
It makes student loans dischargeable for medically distressed debtors, instead of requiring the near-impossible 'undue hardship' showing.

It bars credit bureaus from including a medically distressed debtor's bankruptcy in consumer reports, so an illness-driven discharge would not follow the person into housing, employment, and credit decisions.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors who would recover less in medical bankruptcies: hospitals, medical providers and their collection agencies, credit card and personal lenders, and holders of student debt. Credit bureaus would also lose a category of data they currently sell. Some of these costs could be passed on through higher prices or tighter lending to other borrowers [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill makes it easier to erase debts, including student loans, so lenders and credit card issuers would bear more losses in medical bankruptcies; some of that cost would be passed back to other borrowers through higher prices or tighter lending.

The $250,000 homestead exemption is a generous new shelter that, in states with low exemption limits, would let medically distressed debtors shield substantial home equity that creditors and, ultimately, other borrowers would otherwise recover.

The protections rely on a self-reported statement of medical expenses under penalty of perjury, and the boundary of 'medically distressed' (for example, job loss tied to a national emergency) would require case-by-case judgment that could invite disputes and delay.

The bill addresses bankruptcy after the fact but does nothing to reduce the underlying medical bills themselves; people would still face the debts and would still need to file for bankruptcy to benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: a family that lost income to cancer would no longer have to pass a means test, wait out a credit counseling session, or surrender most of its home equity to keep a bankruptcy case alive, and a discharge would no longer brand them "bankrupt" to every future landlord and lender [S2]. The costs an honest supporter must acknowledge: the bill makes it easier to wipe out debts, so some creditors would charge more or lend less to everyone to cover the added risk, and the generous new exemptions could be engineered by debtors who plan medical spending around the three-year lookback window despite the perjury attestation [S2]. The bill also does nothing about the root cause — it treats the symptom, leaving the medical billing and insurance system that produces the debt untouched. And as introduced, its biggest weakness is political: it has not attracted enough support to get a hearing, let alone a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 14, 2026 and sent to two House committees, but neither committee has taken it up, and with one cosponsor it is unlikely to reach a floor vote before this Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on July 14, 2026 and referred to the Judiciary Committee and the Financial Services Committee.
As of the latest record it has one cosponsor, Rep. André Carson, and the action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action.

The bill would create a new class of 'medically distressed debtor' and, for those debtors, raise the home-equity exemption to $250,000, waive the Chapter 7 means test and Chapter 13 repayment requirements, skip credit counseling, allow student loans to be discharged, and keep the bankruptcy off consumer credit reports.
With the Congress set to end on January 3, 2027, a bill referred to two committees with a single cosponsor and no scheduled action faces long odds of advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because nothing has happened, the current bankruptcy rules stay in place: creditors, debt collectors, and credit bureaus keep the present system in which medical debt is collected under normal terms and medical bankruptcies appear on credit reports. People facing medical debt get no new relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Creditors and collectors; no relief arrived

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats, Reps. Cohen and Carson, are on the record supporting the bill, and no member of either party has voted or spoken against it; the record shows no partisan fight because the bill has not moved.

industries.note: Medical debt is a major revenue source for collection agencies; easier discharges and lower repayment obligations for medically distressed debtors would erase balances they currently collect. Their gain normally comes at the expense of sick people's remaining assets and income.

Medical debts are usually owed to hospitals and providers rather than card issuers, but easier discharges and bigger homestead exemptions increase creditor losses in these cases. Some cost would likely be spread to other borrowers through pricing.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: The bill removes a whole class of bankruptcy entries from the files these companies sell to lenders and landlords. Removing the data slightly shrinks their product, though the effect is modest.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and the federal student loan portfolio
industries.note: Medically distressed debtors could discharge student loans without proving undue hardship, shifting some losses onto loan holders. Today that debt is effectively non-dischargeable, so servicers' interest runs against borrowers here.

The bill does not change how providers bill, but uncollected medical balances would be more likely to vanish in bankruptcy, increasing provider bad debt. Providers' interest in aggressive billing and collections runs against patients in debt.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits at the starting line: referred to two committees with a single cosponsor and no hearings, markups, or committee votes on the record. With less than six months left in this Congress, the standard path for a bill like this is to die in committee at the end of the session. Advancing would require the Judiciary or Financial Services chair to schedule action and the bill to attract many more cosponsors, including from the majority party; nothing in the record suggests either is happening.
